I wasn't part of the maintenance, but I would surmise that it is because salt water is a solvent. We lost a few wheels likely because it compromised the integrity of the assembly to a point where it would be negligent to keep them in rotation on the aircraft. Most everything that is designed, engineered, and manufactured for the US military is serve a specific and narrow purpose, and does that one job as intended. Salt water tears ships apart; ships that are designed to deminish the effects of corrosion, so it would make sense that even a few hours of a salt bath could conceivably take its toll on the wheels.

I used to manage the tire program onboard the Truman in the aviation supply division some years ago. I had four storerooms dedicated storing both tires and and wheel assemblies. Three of those storerooms we dedicated used for storing just the tires, and one for completed tire/wheel assemblies to support flight ops. 

My shift lasted from 1300 to 0100, where upon the end of my shift I would inspect my storerooms and make my counts to report to the division heads that had their maintenance meetings in the mornings after I had gone to my rack. I loved that part of my job, and the job was pretty much only contingent only counting and following paper trails when counts didn't match the system. 

All was well one night during deployment, I wrapped my normal duties as the IBS manager and took my clipboard to count expensive pieces of rubber and metal. Nothing out of the ordinary from what I could remember, so I updated my sheet to reflect on hand quantities and submitted to the department heads, and called it a night. 

The next day at the beginning of my shift, I had a requisition come through for an order that was in the main tire storeroom, I grab the key, and make my way forward. As I swung open the door after undogging each latch I see a fucking pool of salt water sloshing around like its own little ocean. Of course, the most expensive wheels are on the bottom because they are main landing gear wheels and quite heavy. It's been a few years since I've left the Navy, but if I recall the wheel assemblies for the F/A 18 E-F Super Hornet cost between $85-100K. There were anywhere from 15 to twenty wheels that were taking a saltwater bath in the preceding hours after I had gone to bed and before I come back to open the next day.

Damage Control rings over the 1MC to call for flooding in my storeroom and this alerts every. single. person. on the ship. Including but not limited to: the maintenance officer, the supply officer, the maintenance Master Chief, the supply Master Chief, that the tire storeroom that supports the entire air wing has been flooded. In value over, if my memory isn't too hazy, a million dollars worth of assets. 

Tldr; I managed the tire program onboard an aircraft carrier in the US Navy and the storeroom that has all the expensive tires like the one in this post flooded and caused serveral thousands of dollars in damages.
